item.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
choices: how a scorebook entry exposed a mis-set clock
how a chess club's junior section grew in size
how a young player upset a former club champion
how a club director learned to set chess clocks
how a scorekeeper came to keep the club's ledger
item.passage:
Every January the Harlow Chess Club rents the basement of the Grange hall for its winter tournament, and every January since I turned thirteen I have kept the scorebook. It is a green ledger with a cracked spine, and in it I write the pairings, the results, and the time each game ends, copied off the wall clock above the coffee urn. Mrs. Lindqvist, who runs the club, says the book is the only thing in the building that remembers anything correctly.

This year's crop of juniors was the largest anyone could recall: eleven kids from the middle school, most of them still learning to write their moves down without glancing up for help. The best of them was Tess Amundsen, who was twelve and played with her chin on her fists, as if the board might tell her something if she got close enough. In the third round she drew Walt Garvey.

Mr. Garvey had been club champion four times and found a way to mention it in most conversations. He arrived early that morning and offered to set all the clocks to thirty minutes a side, which Mrs. Lindqvist let him do because it saved her twenty minutes. During his game with Tess he leaned back between moves and hummed. Twice he reached across to straighten one of her pawns while her clock was running, a habit that cost her seconds she badly needed and cost him nothing at all.

Tess lost on time at move thirty-eight. Mr. Garvey shook her hand, signed her scoresheet before she had finished reading it, and went to refill his coffee. I wrote the result in the book, and then the time, 11:38, and my pencil stopped. The round had begun at 11:00 sharp, and the clock on the table still showed Mr. Garvey with eighteen minutes left. Twelve minutes of his and thirty of hers made forty-two, and only thirty-eight had passed.

I carried the book to Mrs. Lindqvist and showed her the two numbers. She picked up the clock, turned it over, and found that Tess's side had been set to twenty-six minutes. Mr. Garvey said his thumb must have slipped on the dial, but it was the kind of slip a person makes only after he has decided that winning matters more than playing the game he signed up for.

Mrs. Lindqvist ruled that the game would be replayed after lunch, on clocks she set herself. Mr. Garvey won the replay in forty minutes, fairly, and Tess shook his hand and went to find her mother. I wrote the new time in the book, 1:47, and drew a single neat line through the old one, so that anyone who opened the ledger later could still read what had been there.
item.explanation: "how a scorebook entry exposed a mis-set clock" is correct: the time the narrator writes in the book shows that "Twelve minutes of his and thirty of hers made forty-two, and only thirty-eight had passed," and the clock turns out to have been "set to twenty-six minutes."

item.passage:
The start of the Pinecrest orienteering meet was a folding table at the edge of a gravel lot, and by the time my sister and I reached it, the fog had swallowed the far end of the lot, the parked cars, and most of the man handing out maps. Maren was sixteen and had run this course twice. I was eleven, her only brother, and had run it once, on a clear day, holding on to her sleeve.

She spread the map on her knee and traced the route with one finger: nine controls, each an orange-and-white flag hung somewhere in the woods with a punch clipped beside it. "Bear left at the split boulder," she said, tapping a small black triangle. "Then follow the stream until the ground rises." I nodded as if I could already picture the boulder, though all I could see was gray.

The fog was the kind that moves. It drifted between the trunks in slow sheets, and every tree I picked out as a landmark had dissolved by the time I reached it, so that I kept turning around to make sure the trail was still behind me. Sounds came from the wrong directions. Somewhere a whistle blew twice, and I would have sworn it was on my left, then on my right, then nowhere at all.

Maren walked with the compass flat on her palm and talked to it under her breath, the way she talks to our dog. She found the boulder, then the stream, then the first four flags, punching our card at each one with a small click that I began to wait for. At the fifth control she let me hold the compass. The needle swung, settled, and swung again whenever my hand shook, and I gripped it so hard that the plastic edge left a red line across my fingers.

Between the sixth and seventh controls the stream split in two. Maren studied the map, said we had drifted too far east, and went back to count paces from the last bend while I waited beside a fallen birch. For about a minute I could hear her counting and see nothing but the white shape of the birch, and I kept one hand on its bark as if the fog might take that next. Then her orange vest came back out of the gray, and she was already pointing upward, at a flag hanging from a branch ten feet above my head.

We finished ninth in our age group. On the drive home the fog lifted off the fields in long strips, and Maren fell asleep against the window with the map still folded in her lap. I kept the punch card. It is in my desk drawer now, nine small holes punched in a crooked row.

"Bear left at the split boulder," she said, tapping a small black triangle. "Then follow the stream until the ground rises." I nodded as if I could already picture the boulder, though all I could see was gray.

The fog was the kind that moves. It drifted between the trunks in slow sheets, and every tree I picked out as a landmark had dissolved by the time I reached it, so that I kept turning around to make sure the trail was still behind me. Sounds came from the wrong directions. Somewhere a whistle blew twice, and I would have sworn it was on my left, then on my right, then nowhere at all.

Maren walked with the compass flat on her palm and talked to it under her breath, the way she talks to our dog. She found the boulder, then the stream, then the first four flags, punching our card at each one with a small click that I began to wait for. At the fifth control she let me hold the compass. The needle swung, settled, and swung again whenever my hand shook, and I gripped it so hard that the plastic edge left a red line across my fingers.

Between the sixth and seventh controls the stream split in two. Maren studied the map, said we had drifted too far east, and went back to count paces from the last bend while I waited beside a fallen birch. For about a minute I could hear her counting and see nothing but the white shape of the birch, and I kept one hand on its bark as if the fog might take that next. Then her orange vest came back out of the gray, and she was already pointing upward, at a flag hanging from a branch ten feet above my head.

We finished ninth in our age group. On the drive home the fog lifted off the fields in long strips, and Maren fell asleep against the window with the map still folded in her lap. I kept the punch card. It is in my desk drawer now, nine small holes punched in a crooked row.

Between the sixth and seventh controls the stream split in two. Then her orange vest came back out of the gray, and she was already pointing upward, at a flag hanging from a branch ten feet above my head.

item.passage:
The 14 leaves the depot at eleven-forty
with its windows fogged from the inside
and a driver named Carmen, who keeps
a thermos wedged beside the fare box.
I take the seat behind the rear door,
where the heater breathes against my shins.

By Delmore Street the traffic is light:
a taxi, a van, a second taxi, then the long
green wave of signals changing for nobody.
The laundromat on Pruitt is still open,
two women folding a sheet between them
as carefully as a flag after a ceremony.

A notice taped above the windows says
that in March the 14 will be folded
into the 12, which runs on the hour
and turns at the hospital instead of the river.
Carmen read it aloud the first night it went up,
then pressed the corner where the tape had lifted
and smoothed it flat again with her thumb.

I have ridden this loop for six winters,
and already I catch myself looking at each stop
the way you look at a house
you have just agreed to sell.

At the river the bus swings wide
past the shuttered ice-cream stand,
and for one block the whole city
hangs upside down in the black water,
streetlights and all, keeping pace with us.

In March that block of river
will go on holding the city upside down
with only the gulls to look at it,
and I will miss it every night at eleven-forty.

Carmen calls the last stop, my stop,
the way she always has, like a question,
and I step down into the cold
and stand at the curb until her taillights
turn the corner at Ash Street and are gone.

The 14 leaves the depot at eleven-forty
with its windows fogged from the inside
and a driver named Carmen, who keeps
a thermos wedged beside the fare box.
I take the seat behind the rear door,
where the heater breathes against my shins.

By Delmore Street the traffic is light:
a taxi, a van, a second taxi, then the long
green wave of signals changing for nobody.
The laundromat on Pruitt is still open,
two women folding a sheet between them
as carefully as a flag after a ceremony.

A notice taped above the windows says
that in March the 14 will be folded
into the 12, which runs on the hour
and turns at the hospital instead of the river.
Carmen read it aloud the first night it went up,
then pressed the corner where the tape had lifted
and smoothed it flat again with her thumb.

I have ridden this loop for six winters,
and already I catch myself looking at each stop
the way you look at a house
you have just agreed to sell.

At the river the bus swings wide
past the shuttered ice-cream stand,
and for one block the whole city
hangs upside down in the black water,
streetlights and all, keeping pace with us.

In March that block of river
will go on holding the city upside down
with only the gulls to look at it,
and I will miss it every night at eleven-forty.

Carmen calls the last stop, my stop,
the way she always has, like a question,
and I step down into the cold
and stand at the curb until her taillights
turn the corner at Ash Street and are gone.

item.prompt: The poem is primarily concerned with
choices: a village pond freezing and its first skaters
an old man testing a pond's ice for safety
one winter day in a village, dawn to dusk
a skating race held on a village pond
a village pond thawing after a long freeze
item.passage:
In the second week of December
the pond behind the Mallory place
stiffens at the edges first,
a gray rim thin as a fingernail
that the ducks walk out on and back.

By Thursday the middle has closed,
and the reeds stand up through it
like pencils left in plaster.
Tom Wick goes out at noon
with an auger and a folding rule,
drills three holes, measures each one twice,
and says "Five inches" to his dog.

He drives a post into the bank
where the brook comes in and the ice stays soft,
and ties a strip of red flannel to the top
so the children will know where to turn.

The first ones out are the Danforth girls,
eight and ten, in their brother's old hockey skates,
and they go the way a sentence goes
when the writer finally knows what she means,
long and sure and all the way to the far shore.

Then the Okafor twins, then a man in a suit coat
who must have left his car running on the road,
then Mrs. Hale, who is seventy-one
and skates backward with her hands behind her,
cutting one clean circle inside another.
She is the one I watch longest every year,
because she makes the whole pond look as if it froze for her.

By four the sun is down behind the barn,
and the skaters go home one by one,
leaving the long white scratches of the afternoon
crossed and recrossed on the darkening ice,
and the red flannel at the brook's mouth
lifting a little in the wind.

choices: how a pen pal's letters changed what the narrator noticed

item.passage:
In the fall of seventh grade, Mrs. Halvorsen walked down the rows handing each of us a slip of paper with a name and an address on it. We would be writing to that person, she said, until June. Mine read Marta Coelho, followed by a town on the coast of Portugal so small that I had to find it with a magnifying glass on the classroom map. The program supplied envelopes, airmail stickers, and a list of suggested topics: family, school, hobbies, food.

My first letter followed the list exactly. I was a boy of twelve with two older brothers. I played the clarinet, badly. My favorite food was spaghetti. The whole thing fit on half a sheet, and I remember being pleased with how efficiently I had covered everything.

Marta's reply ran to four pages, and she skipped the list altogether. She described her walk to school, which took her past a fish auction that opened at seven, a wall where an old man repainted the same blue door every spring, and a café whose owner set out exactly four chairs each morning and carried them in again at noon. Her grandfather, she added, made a mean fish soup, and half the street found some reason to drop by on Fridays when the pot was on. She could take the most ordinary twenty minutes of her week and set them down so exactly that I felt I had walked them beside her. I read the letter three times on the bus home, trying to work out how she had done it.

My second letter was much harder to write. I had nothing that seemed worth four pages, so I began to pay attention. I noticed that the crossing guard outside our school whistled the same three notes every time he stepped into the road. I noticed that the custodian, Mr. Ruiz, kept tomato plants growing in coffee cans along the boiler-room window and gave each can a quarter turn every afternoon. I started carrying a notebook so that by Sunday night I would have a week's worth of these things ready to send.

By spring my letters were as long as hers, and they had stopped being about me. They were about Mr. Ruiz and his tomatoes, the crossing guard's three notes, the smell of the gym floor after it was waxed. Marta answered every one with questions, wanting to know which way the tomatoes leaned and whether the three notes were the start of a song. Even now I think she was the finest observer I have ever known, and she was twelve years old.

We still write, though mostly by email now, and less often than we did that year. Last month she sent a photograph of the old man's door, painted a new and deeper blue. I printed it and pinned it above my desk, beside a page from that first notebook, and some mornings I catch myself reading the street outside my window the way she taught me to, one small particular at a time.

In the fall of seventh grade, Mrs. Halvorsen walked down the rows handing each of us a slip of paper with a name and an address on it. We would be writing to that person, she said, until June. Mine read Marta Coelho, followed by a town on the coast of Portugal so small that I had to find it with a magnifying glass on the classroom map. The program supplied envelopes, airmail stickers, and a list of suggested topics: family, school, hobbies, food.

My first letter followed the list exactly. I was a boy of twelve with two older brothers. I played the clarinet, badly. My favorite food was spaghetti. The whole thing fit on half a sheet, and I remember being pleased with how efficiently I had covered everything.

Marta's reply ran to four pages, and she skipped the list altogether. She described her walk to school, which took her past a fish auction that opened at seven, a wall where an old man repainted the same blue door every spring, and a café whose owner set out exactly four chairs each morning and carried them in again at noon. Her grandfather, she added, made a mean fish soup, and half the street found some reason to drop by on Fridays when the pot was on. She could take the most ordinary twenty minutes of her week and set them down so exactly that I felt I had walked them beside her. I read the letter three times on the bus home, trying to work out how she had done it.

My second letter was much harder to write. I had nothing that seemed worth four pages, so I began to pay attention. I noticed that the crossing guard outside our school whistled the same three notes every time he stepped into the road. I noticed that the custodian, Mr. Ruiz, kept tomato plants growing in coffee cans along the boiler-room window and gave each can a quarter turn every afternoon. I started carrying a notebook so that by Sunday night I would have a week's worth of these things ready to send.

By spring my letters were as long as hers, and they had stopped being about me. They were about Mr. Ruiz and his tomatoes, the crossing guard's three notes, the smell of the gym floor after it was waxed. Marta answered every one with questions, wanting to know which way the tomatoes leaned and whether the three notes were the start of a song. Even now I think she was the finest observer I have ever known, and she was twelve years old.

We still write, though mostly by email now, and less often than we did that year. Last month she sent a photograph of the old man's door, painted a new and deeper blue. I printed it and pinned it above my desk, beside a page from that first notebook, and some mornings I catch myself reading the street outside my window the way she taught me to, one small particular at a time.

The lighting board at Fairview High lived in a plywood booth at the back of the auditorium, up a ladder that swayed slightly when you climbed it. It was older than any of us on the crew: a gray metal case with twelve sliders in a row, a master fader at the end, and a strip of masking tape above each slider where someone had written, in pencil, what it controlled. FRONT WASH. BLUE SKY. STAIRS. Some of the labels had been erased and rewritten so many times that the tape had worn through.

I joined the crew in ninth grade because a friend had, and Priya Nair, the senior who ran the booth, put me on the board because nobody else wanted it. She taught me in a single afternoon. Each cue was a set of slider positions written on an index card, and my job was to move the sliders from one card to the next at the speed she called through my headset. 'A four-count fade,' she would say, 'is four full counts.'

By opening night of The Winter Queen I had learned the board's habits. Slider seven caught at the halfway mark and had to be eased past it. The master fader ran smooth as water. In the second act the queen made a long entrance down a staircase while I brought up the amber light behind her over a slow ten-count, so that she seemed to arrive with the dawn.

On the second night the queen's velvet train snagged on a nail at the top of the staircase. She stopped, and for a moment the whole auditorium waited with her. Priya's voice came quietly through the headset: 'Hold.' I held, my hand flat on the sliders, while a lady-in-waiting knelt and worked the velvet loose, and when the queen moved again I finished the ten-count from exactly where I had stopped.

The school replaced the board two years after I graduated. The new console is a laptop and a small panel of buttons, and it can store four hundred cues and run them on its own. When I went back for the spring musical last year, the laptop sat on the shelf where the board had been, its screen glowing blue in the dark. I stood in the doorway of the booth for a long time, missing the old board the way you miss a person who used to sit in one particular chair.

I understand why they changed it. The new system is better in every way that can be measured, and no student will have to coax slider seven past its catch again. Still, I would give a great deal to rest my fingers on those twelve worn sliders one more time and bring the house slowly down to black.

item.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Most adults remember their childhood drives as ordeals.
Children today expect more stimulation than past children did.
Tablets help families keep the peace on long car journeys.
Boredom on long drives gives children valuable time to think.
Families should take fewer long drives with young children.
item.passage:
Every summer, on highways across the country, the same scene repeats itself. A family loads the car for a six-hour drive to a grandparent's house or a lake, and before the car has reached the end of the street, a tablet appears in the back seat, stocked with films and games enough for a drive three times as long. The parents call this keeping the peace.

To hand a child a tablet at the end of the driveway is to decide, before the trip has begun, that six hours of her own thinking are worth less than six hours of someone else's cartoons. I understand the reasoning. A quiet back seat is easier to drive with, and the family car is usually sound enough to go another hundred thousand miles; it is the passengers we doubt can last the afternoon. But the tablet solves a problem that was never a problem, and it charges a steep price for the solution.

That price is boredom, or rather the loss of it. Boredom on a long drive is unpleasant for about the first hour. Then something happens. A child who has run out of things to want begins, slowly, to look. She counts red barns. She invents a family for the people in the next car and gives them a reason to be driving to Ohio. She watches the shadow of the car slide along the guardrail and works out, without anyone explaining it, that it shrinks as noon comes on. These are the hours in which a mind learns to entertain itself, and they cannot be scheduled any other way.

Adults tend to remember long drives as ordeals, and the memory is accurate as far as it goes. What it leaves out is the second half of the ordeal, the part in which the window turned into a screen of its own, one that showed fields and water towers and a horse standing alone in the rain. That screen asks more of its viewer than any film does. It offers nothing until the viewer brings something to it.

The usual objection is that children today expect constant stimulation, and that denying it to them for six hours is a kind of cruelty. The objection has it backward. Children expect constant stimulation because we keep supplying it, and every long drive with the tablet switched on teaches the lesson again. A family that leaves the tablet in the trunk for even one trip will face an hour of complaint and then, very often, a long and surprising quiet.

So pack snacks, pack a map, and pack patience for the first sixty miles. Then let the back seat be dull, and see what the children in it make of the afternoon.

Every summer, on highways across the country, the same scene repeats itself. A family loads the car for a six-hour drive to a grandparent's house or a lake, and before the car has reached the end of the street, a tablet appears in the back seat, stocked with films and games enough for a drive three times as long. The parents call this keeping the peace.

To hand a child a tablet at the end of the driveway is to decide, before the trip has begun, that six hours of her own thinking are worth less than six hours of someone else's cartoons. That price is boredom, or rather the loss of it. Boredom on a long drive is unpleasant for about the first hour. Then something happens. A child who has run out of things to want begins, slowly, to look. She counts red barns. She invents a family for the people in the next car and gives them a reason to be driving to Ohio. She watches the shadow of the car slide along the guardrail and works out, without anyone explaining it, that it shrinks as noon comes on. These are the hours in which a mind learns to entertain itself, and they cannot be scheduled any other way.

item.passage:
On the first Saturday of every month, the community hall on Linden Street becomes a repair cafe and fills with broken things. People arrive carrying toasters with dead elements, lamps that flicker, a radio that hums and refuses to tune, jackets with split seams and torn pockets. They take a number at the door and wait on folding chairs until a volunteer calls them over to one of six long tables, where the tools are laid out on old bath towels.

The volunteers are mostly retired. choices: a manager's decision to replace boys with young women operators
the snowstorm that closed the only road into a mining town

item.passage:
In the spring of 1901, the Harrow Gap Telephone Company rented two rooms above Pell's hardware store and hired five young women to sit before a wooden cabinet studded with brass. The mountain town had perhaps nine hundred residents and forty-one telephones, most of them in shops, the doctor's office and the mine superintendent's house. The company's manager, Arthur Voss, had first hired boys as operators, as the larger cities did, but he dismissed them within a month for arguing with callers and wrestling between calls.

The switchboard worked by hand. Each incoming call tripped a small hinged shutter on the board, which dropped to show the caller's line number. The operator pushed a cord into the jack beneath the shutter, asked "Number, please?", then plugged a second cord into the jack of the line being called and turned a crank to ring it. At noon a busy operator might handle a call every twenty seconds, reaching across a board six feet wide while keeping track of which conversations had ended.

The work demanded more than quick hands. Callers seldom asked for numbers; they asked for "the doctor" or "whoever has the key to the church," and the operators learned every household and its habits. During the snowstorm of February 1907, when drifts closed the only road for nine days, the night operator, Clara Bettendorf, stayed at the board for thirty hours and passed messages between the mine office and families waiting to hear which shafts had been cleared. The superintendent later wrote to the company that she had "kept the whole town in one room." It is hard to read her log from those nine days without marveling at her steadiness.

The job changed the women as well. Operators earned six dollars a week, more than a shop clerk and nearly as much as a schoolteacher, and for many it was the first wage they controlled themselves. In 1911 the day operators asked Voss for a rest period each afternoon and a chair with a back, and after several weeks of letters to the company's head office, they received both. Edna Marsh, who had started at sixteen, later used her savings to open a stationery shop on Main Street.

In 1915 the company replaced the cabinet with a larger board in a brick building across the street and hired eleven operators. By then the town counted more than three hundred telephones. Reading the company's ledgers and the operators' own letters, one is struck by how much those first women carried with so little equipment: a few dozen cords, a crank, and a memory for the voices of a whole valley.

item.passage:
For about sixty years, the most valuable crop around Lake Orrin was harvested in January. Once the ice on the lake's broad north bay had thickened to fourteen inches, the farmers who grew oats and potatoes in summer brought their horses down to the shore, and the Orrin Ice Company paid them a dollar a day and their meals to cut it. In a good season the company stored forty thousand tons.

The work followed a fixed order. First a horse-drawn plow scored the surface into a grid of grooves about twenty-two inches apart. Men with long-toothed saws finished the cuts, and others with iron bars split off whole rows of blocks, which they floated along an open channel to the shore. There a chain conveyor lifted each block, more than two hundred pounds of it, up a ramp and into the ice house. Every mild winter presented the same hazard, ice near the channel thin enough for a horse to break through, and the company kept a coil of rope on every sled for hauling one out.

The ice houses themselves were wooden barns three stories high, with double walls packed with sawdust from the mills upriver. Workers laid the blocks in tight courses and spread more sawdust between the layers and across the top. So insulated, the ice lost less than a third of its weight by the following autumn. Through the summer, railcars lined with straw carried it south to dairies, butcher shops and hotels, and wagons delivered smaller pieces to kitchens in town, where it went into wooden iceboxes lined with zinc.

The trade ended faster than it had grown. Electric refrigerators reached the town's shops in the 1920s and its kitchens in the 1930s, and in 1934 the company cut its last harvest. A few of the old cutters found work at the creamery's new freezing plant; most went back to their farms with one less source of winter income. In 1938 the largest of the ice houses burned, and the company's ledgers burned with it. Losing those ledgers is the hardest part of the story to accept, since they held the names of nearly every man who had cut ice on the lake.

The ice trade left the lake almost exactly as it found it, which is one reason it is so easily forgotten. A cellar hole on the north shore and a few rusted saw blades at the historical society are nearly all that survive. It seems a pity that the people who swim in the north bay each summer have no way of picturing the grid of channels, the steaming horses and the long rows of men that once covered it.

For about sixty years, the most valuable crop around Lake Orrin was harvested in January. Once the ice on the lake's broad north bay had thickened to fourteen inches, the farmers who grew oats and potatoes in summer brought their horses down to the shore, and the Orrin Ice Company paid them a dollar a day and their meals to cut it. In a good season the company stored forty thousand tons.

The work followed a fixed order. First a horse-drawn plow scored the surface into a grid of grooves about twenty-two inches apart. Men with long-toothed saws finished the cuts, and others with iron bars split off whole rows of blocks, which they floated along an open channel to the shore. There a chain conveyor lifted each block, more than two hundred pounds of it, up a ramp and into the ice house. Every mild winter presented the same hazard, ice near the channel thin enough for a horse to break through, and the company kept a coil of rope on every sled for hauling one out.

The ice houses themselves were wooden barns three stories high, with double walls packed with sawdust from the mills upriver. Workers laid the blocks in tight courses and spread more sawdust between the layers and across the top. So insulated, the ice lost less than a third of its weight by the following autumn. Through the summer, railcars lined with straw carried it south to dairies, butcher shops and hotels, and wagons delivered smaller pieces to kitchens in town, where it went into wooden iceboxes lined with zinc.

The trade ended faster than it had grown. Electric refrigerators reached the town's shops in the 1920s and its kitchens in the 1930s, and in 1934 the company cut its last harvest. A few of the old cutters found work at the creamery's new freezing plant; most went back to their farms with one less source of winter income. In 1938 the largest of the ice houses burned, and the company's ledgers burned with it. Losing those ledgers is the hardest part of the story to accept, since they held the names of nearly every man who had cut ice on the lake.

The ice trade left the lake almost exactly as it found it, which is one reason it is so easily forgotten. A cellar hole on the north shore and a few rusted saw blades at the historical society are nearly all that survive. It seems a pity that the people who swim in the north bay each summer have no way of picturing the grid of channels, the steaming horses and the long rows of men that once covered it.

Once the ice on the lake's broad north bay had thickened to fourteen inches, the farmers who grew oats and potatoes in summer brought their horses down to the shore, and the Orrin Ice Company paid them a dollar a day and their meals to cut it. In a good season the company stored forty thousand tons.

The work followed a fixed order. First a horse-drawn plow scored the surface into a grid of grooves about twenty-two inches apart. Men with long-toothed saws finished the cuts, and others with iron bars split off whole rows of blocks, which they floated along an open channel to the shore. There a chain conveyor lifted each block, more than two hundred pounds of it, up a ramp and into the ice house. Every mild winter presented the same hazard, ice near the channel thin enough for a horse to break through, and the company kept a coil of rope on every sled for hauling one out.

The ice houses themselves were wooden barns three stories high, with double walls packed with sawdust from the mills upriver. Workers laid the blocks in tight courses and spread more sawdust between the layers and across the top. So insulated, the ice lost less than a third of its weight by the following autumn. Through the summer, railcars lined with straw carried it south to dairies, butcher shops and hotels, and wagons delivered smaller pieces to kitchens in town, where it went into wooden iceboxes lined with zinc.

The trade ended faster than it had grown. Electric refrigerators reached the town's shops in the 1920s and its kitchens in the 1930s, and in 1934 the company cut its last harvest. A few of the old cutters found work at the creamery's new freezing plant; most went back to their farms with one less source of winter income. In 1938 the largest of the ice houses burned, and the company's ledgers burned with it. Losing those ledgers is the hardest part of the story to accept, since they held the names of nearly every man who had cut ice on the lake.

The ice trade left the lake almost exactly as it found it, which is one reason it is so easily forgotten. A cellar hole on the north shore and a few rusted saw blades at the historical society are nearly all that survive. It seems a pity that the people who swim in the north bay each summer have no way of picturing the grid of channels, the steaming horses and the long rows of men that once covered it.

item.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
choices: the dating of old gravestones in a city's two cemeteries
a botanist's use of lichens to trace the air of a city
the effects of burning coal on the air across a region

item.passage:
When Helen Sarrow began walking the streets of Calder with a hand lens in 1979, the city held no measurements of its air from before the previous decade. Sarrow, a botanist at the municipal college who had paid her board through graduate school by tutoring chemistry, believed the record existed anyway, written in lichen on the bark of the city's trees and the faces of its gravestones.

A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and an alga, and it takes almost everything it needs from rain and air. Because it has no roots to filter what arrives, it absorbs whatever the air carries, including the sulfur dioxide given off by burning coal. Species differ greatly in how much of that gas they can bear. Flat, crusty lichens survive in dirty air; leafy kinds disappear as it worsens; and the bushy, branching species vanish first. By noting which kinds grow on a tree, a trained observer can rank the air around it roughly, without any instrument.

Sarrow surveyed more than six hundred street trees, and her map showed a ring. Within a mile of the Fenwick power station, which had burned coal since 1921, the bark held only a gray crust. Leafy lichens appeared beyond the ring, and branching ones grew only in the hill parks at the edge of the city.

The gravestones gave her something the trees lacked: dates. A stone carved in 1890 cannot carry a lichen older than 1890, and many common species widen at a steady rate on stone, a little more than a millimeter a year. By measuring the largest patches in Calder's two oldest cemeteries, Sarrow could estimate when each had begun to grow. The result surprised her. Nearly all the leafy patches, even on stones from the 1850s, were less than eight years old. They had started around 1972, the year Fenwick switched from coal to gas.

In 1981 Sarrow took her findings to the city council and asked for air monitors near the rail yards, where a cluster of trees still carried nothing but crust. The council's reply, a two-line letter calling her work "a study of moss on tombstones," treated careful evidence as a curiosity. Monitors were installed only in 1990, after the state required them, and their first year of readings put the rail yards among the worst sites in the region. It is difficult to excuse a council that waited for its own instruments to report what the lichens had shown a decade earlier.

choices: Changing the legs of an ant causes it to lose its sense of direction.

item.passage:
On the white crust of the Kessra salt flat, a foraging ant may wander more than a hundred meters from its nest, zigzagging in search of insects killed by the heat. When it finds one, it turns and runs home in a nearly straight line, stopping within a few centimeters of an entrance about the width of a pencil. There are few more impressive journeys in the insect world than that short run home. The flat offers no landmarks to steer by, and scent trails bake away in minutes. For two field seasons, the biologists Lena Hartigan and Tomas Riel set out to learn how the ants managed it.

Direction, they knew, came largely from the sun. Earlier workers had shown that an ant keeps track of the sun's angle as it walks, adding up every turn. Hartigan checked this with a large mirror held above the ants' path: when the mirror hid the real sun and showed a reflected one from the opposite side, homeward ants promptly reversed course and ran away from the nest. Distance was the harder question. Without a landmark, how could an ant know when it had gone far enough?

Riel suspected the ants were, in effect, counting their steps. To test the idea, the pair trained ants to walk to a feeder ten meters from the nest along a straight aluminum channel. Then, at the feeder, they changed the ants' legs. For one group, Riel glued a short bristle to each leg, lengthening the stride like a pair of stilts. For another, he trimmed the legs slightly, shortening it. Each ant was then moved to a parallel channel and allowed to head for home.

If the ants measured distance by steps, the stilted ants should overshoot the nest and the trimmed ants should stop short. That is exactly what happened. The stilted ants ran about fifteen meters before beginning the tight circles an ant makes when searching for its entrance; the trimmed ants began circling at about six. Ants whose legs had been left alone stopped at ten.

The surprise came the next day. Ants that had walked out to the feeder already wearing their bristles, and then walked home on them, also stopped at ten meters. Whatever the ants were counting, they had counted it on the way out with the same legs, so the error vanished. That result became the pair's most useful lead, and it sent them to study how an ant's stride changes on soft sand and on slopes. It is remarkable that a brain smaller than a grain of salt can do this arithmetic at a run, on ground hot enough to kill it within minutes.

item.prompt: The author's attitude toward the desert ants is best described as
choices: mournful
scornful
anxious
admiring
whimsical
item.passage:
On the white crust of the Kessra salt flat, a foraging ant may wander more than a hundred meters from its nest, zigzagging in search of insects killed by the heat. When it finds one, it turns and runs home in a nearly straight line, stopping within a few centimeters of an entrance about the width of a pencil. There are few more impressive journeys in the insect world than that short run home. The flat offers no landmarks to steer by, and scent trails bake away in minutes. For two field seasons, the biologists Lena Hartigan and Tomas Riel set out to learn how the ants managed it.

Direction, they knew, came largely from the sun. Earlier workers had shown that an ant keeps track of the sun's angle as it walks, adding up every turn. Hartigan checked this with a large mirror held above the ants' path: when the mirror hid the real sun and showed a reflected one from the opposite side, homeward ants promptly reversed course and ran away from the nest. Distance was the harder question. Without a landmark, how could an ant know when it had gone far enough?

Riel suspected the ants were, in effect, counting their steps. To test the idea, the pair trained ants to walk to a feeder ten meters from the nest along a straight aluminum channel. Then, at the feeder, they changed the ants' legs. For one group, Riel glued a short bristle to each leg, lengthening the stride like a pair of stilts. For another, he trimmed the legs slightly, shortening it. Each ant was then moved to a parallel channel and allowed to head for home.

If the ants measured distance by steps, the stilted ants should overshoot the nest and the trimmed ants should stop short. That is exactly what happened. The stilted ants ran about fifteen meters before beginning the tight circles an ant makes when searching for its entrance; the trimmed ants began circling at about six. Ants whose legs had been left alone stopped at ten.

The surprise came the next day. Ants that had walked out to the feeder already wearing their bristles, and then walked home on them, also stopped at ten meters. Whatever the ants were counting, they had counted it on the way out with the same legs, so the error vanished. That result became the pair's most useful lead, and it sent them to study how an ant's stride changes on soft sand and on slopes. It is remarkable that a brain smaller than a grain of salt can do this arithmetic at a run, on ground hot enough to kill it within minutes.
